chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from Abu Jamilyah, from Amr ibn Hurayth, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him, said:

I asked him about a man who said: If he spoke to a relative of his, then upon him is the journey to the House of God, and all that he owns in the way of God, and he is free from the religion of Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family). He said: He should fast for three days, and give charity to ten poor people. The approach in this narration is to interpret it as recommended (mustahabb), or that he makes that as gratitude to God by opposing His disobedience, rather than it being an expiation (kaffarah), in contrast to a vow, and this is confirmed.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a vow to travel to the Kaaba if one speaks to a relative?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling in the chapter 'No Vow in Disobedience,' where Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that a vow to travel to the Kaaba upon speaking to a relative is interpreted as recommended gratitude (shukr) rather than a mandatory expiation (kaffarah). This distinction highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that such vows are not strictly binding as penalties for sin, but rather acts of voluntary devotion, contrasting with the stricter obligations of formal vows (nadhr).
